John Moses and Joseph Kirkland (eds.), History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 1 (Chicago and New York: Munsell & Co., 1895). Read here for the town before 1836: the immigration chapter 'From Village to City - 1830 to 1837 - the Balloon Age' at printed pages 78-79 and 87-101, the early taverns and hotels at pages 560-561, the 'Real Estate and Insurance' chapter at pages 541-542, the packing trade at page 389, the fire department at pages 207-208, the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy quoted from Blanchard at page 35, and the Biographical sketches of P. F. W. Peck, Philo Carpenter, John Dean Caton and Alexander N. Fullerton at pages 570-577 and 584; and, for the shore of 1812 (T-0471), the chapter 'The Massacre' at pages 49-50, 54 and 60-61 - the low, discontinuous sand-hills south of Twelfth Street, the scattered cottonwoods on the bank's lower reaches, and the two 'Massacre trees' of Eighteenth Street with Mrs. Kinzie's word that they were saplings in 1812.

transcribes.note: PRINTED AT LENGTH AND NOT MERELY CITED. At pages 34-35 the volume introduces the Kinzie and Clybourn genealogy as 'best told by Rufus Blanchard ... He says:' and sets the whole passage as a block quotation, which is why bk_mose1_019 - Benjamin Hall's 1830 arrival and the town's first tannery - is a reading of Blanchard through Moses and Kirkland and not of Moses and Kirkland. This project does not hold Blanchard and cannot check the transcription. Blanchard in turn credits Benjamin Hall himself for the detail, so the chain to the fact is three deep and the claim says so.

what_it_does_not_supply: MOST OF WHAT IT WAS FETCHED FOR. Of the forty-nine lead surnames the Newberry index flagged against this work, thirteen earned a claim, twenty-one appear only outside the pre-1836 window, eight appear early and say nothing usable, one (`black`) is only ever the adjective, four are unresolved because the volume carries a surname one character from the index card's spelling, and two are absent outright. The full row-by-row result is committed at data/research/books/moses_kirkland_v1_lead_surnames.json so the next run does not pay for the search twice.

VOLUME 2, WHICH IS HALF THE WORK. Only volume 1 is read. The Newberry cards do not say which volume they cite, so an absence recorded here may simply be in the other book, and every ABSENT verdict in the lookup file says so on itself.

AN INDEPENDENT VOICE. It is a compilation of 1895 and it names its own authorities on the pages read: Andreas for Garrett's $1,800,000 of auction sales, Bross's History of Chicago page 38 for the earliest deeds, the Story of Chicago page 130 for Caton's election tally, Hurlbut's Chicago Antiquities pages 37-8 for the pre-1830 settler list, S. R. Beggs's West and Northwest page 95 for the Black Hawk alarm, and Rufus Blanchard's Discovery of the Northwest and History of Chicago (1881) quoted at length for the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy. Where the sentence itself credits another work, the claim says so and the citation must go to that work and not to this one.
A SINGLE ADDRESS IN THE MODERN SENSE, and no street numbers. Positions here are corners, lots, blocks, a river bank and a tree.

ANY DATE FINER THAN THE YEAR for two things this project wanted finer: Caton's marriage, which is given as '1835' with the scene date sitting in the middle of it, and the Hubbard-Marsh packing partnership, which is 'later'.

CONSISTENCY WITH ITSELF. Page 89 dates Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings to 1832 while page 570 has Peck's occupied in the fall of 1831; page 207 forms the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company on 7 October 1835 while page 570 has it organised on 20 October 1835. Both readings of each are recorded and neither is adopted.
what_it_supplies: A TRADE CENSUS OF THE WHOLE TOWN, at page 95: the State census taken between 1 September and December 1835 counted 3,297 people, forty-four stores, two book stores, four druggists, two silversmiths and jewellers, two tin and copper manufactories, two printing offices, two breweries, one steam saw-mill, one iron foundry, four storage and forwarding houses, eight taverns, one lottery office, one bank, five churches, seven schools, twenty-two lawyers, fourteen physicians, and a lyceum and reading room. The project had no denominator for its business layer and this is one - for December 1835 and not for July.

A BUILDING WITH FOUR OF THE FIVE FIELDS data/structures/ WANTS, at page 90: John S. C. Hogan's story-and-a-half log storehouse, 45 by 18 feet, at the angle where Lake and South Water streets meet, with the post office partitioned off inside it from 2 November 1832.

TWO RESIDENCES STATED AS SUCH, which is the field the town is thinnest in: Rev. Jeremiah Porter lodging and keeping his study in the second storey of Peck's store from May 1833 (page 571), and John Dean Caton renting the back room and attic of Dr Temple's Temple Building from December 1833, sleeping in the attic and practising law in the back room, and sub-letting desk-room in it to his competitor Spring (page 577).

BUSINESSES GIVEN BY CORNER, LOT OR LANDMARK: Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings at the south-east corners of South Water and Dearborn and of South Water and La Salle (page 89); Peck's two-storey frame store of black walnut brought from Detroit, occupied in the fall of 1831 (page 570); Sylvester Marsh killing beef under an old elm on the open prairie at what became Monroe Street from the winter of 1833-4 (page 389); William Jones's lots 2 and 7 in block 17 fronting Water and Lake (page 542).

OCCUPATIONS AND ARRIVALS for men this project already holds: Philo Carpenter as the town's first druggist, arriving within a month before 19 August 1832; Benjamin Hall as proprietor of the first tannery ever established there, arriving 1830; Dole, Clybourn, the Noble brothers and Gurdon S. Hubbard beginning the slaughtering and packing trade in 1832; the 1833 spring arrivals including Caton, Kimball and Asahel Pierce; and Hubbard's permanent residence dated to 1832 by the compiler's own reason for leaving him off a list.

TWO PRESENCE LISTS: the twenty-two men who signed the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company roll on 7 October 1835 (pages 207-208), and, unread and left for its own ticket, the 'LIST OF ACTUAL SETTLERS AT CHICAGO, PRIOR TO 1830' at pages 78-79, about thirty rows with nativity, year and remarks columns.
ONE STATEMENT ABOUT THE GROUND OF THE SCENE, at page 79: the winter of 1834-5 was open, with little snow, front doors standing open all winter, and cattle living on grass on the river bank.

endings.text: Back up the stairs over Jones & King's with ink on your fingers and two papers' news in your head: what the American is selling against the cholera, and what came up the river through the draw. Nobody asked you to look at either. An apprentice who notices may one day be the one who writes it up, or the one who decides what is left out.

Back to the office with an empty arm and the river in your head: the Sauganash read first, the sails at the draw last. The Democrat comes out again next Wednesday. If the cholera comes up the river with one of those sails, it will be in that number too.

Every copy delivered, and both papers read before noon: the American's elixir at one end of the morning, the auction's first sale at the other. Fear and money, the two things that sell a paper in July. Upstairs over Jones & King's there is type to clean and a week to fill.

The round is done: the Sauganash first, the Tremont last, every copy delivered before noon. Upstairs over Jones & King's, next week's type is waiting. Six weeks ago you answered a notice for an apprentice; this morning the town read, in the paper you carried, how healthy it was.

evidence.reasoning: Read off the issue numbers this project already cites from the same transcription: 20 May 1835 is Vol. II No. 5, 27 May No. 6, 10 June No. 8, 24 June No. 10 and 1 July No. 11. The numbers advance by one for every seven days, and 1 July 1835 fell on a Wednesday, so each of those dates is a Wednesday. No masthead statement of the paper's terms or day of issue has been read for this claim.
evidence.text: The Democrat came out once a week, on Wednesdays, and the number dated 1 July 1835 is No. 11 of its second volume.

It was the first drawbridge across the river.

evidence.text: Alanson Sweet built the first Tremont House, a frame building, in 1833 on the north-west corner of Lake and Dearborn streets. Ira Couch took the house in 1834, and Andreas names the Couch brothers among its keepers before it burned on 27 October 1839.

evidence.locator: p. 561, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 98839-98872 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)
evidence.text: In the early 1830s Alanson Sweet opened a saloon and boarding house at the north-west corner of Lake and Dearborn, 'the nucleus of the present Tremont House'; its brick successor of 1850 was thought 'absurdly large', and people called it Couch's Folly.

evidence.locator: 24 June 1835 (Vol. II No. 10), p. 3, col. 3 (transcription lines 2540–2559, interleaved; extracted claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_24#c008). Transcription-mediated reading; the auctioneer’s surname reads MONTGOMERY and his initials are lost. The American’s 27 June copy of the notice is ambiguous between the first and the last day of July, so only the Democrat’s reading is used.
evidence.text: A notice headed ‘[Auction an]d Commission House’ announces a store taken on South Water Street for auction and commission business, its first public sale to be held ‘the 1st day of July’, which is the scene date.

evidence.reasoning: Uses the existing structure records' scene-date phases and positions, as the published jaunts that stop at these places do (News Before Breakfast, Along the Working Harbor, Work on the Waterfront). The printing office's business record reads South Water Street and nothing narrower, so the jaunt starts at the corner it left. The notices are read from the papers, not from the places.
evidence.text: The six places are exterior stops in the 1 July 1835 scene. The Democrat's corner is visited as its former office, and the office over Jones & King's hardware, which the paper names only by its street, is not placed in the town; the American's office is placed near the drawbridge and Newberry & Dole's house on a disputed bank. No interior, front door, keeper or reader on the morning is claimed.

The apprentice the visitor plays, their age and duties, the bundle of papers and the round it is carried on, the order of the route, the choices, the four endings, the timing inputs and the An Apprentice's Round keepsake are invented connective narrative. The Democrat's notice for an apprentice is real (20 May 1835); who answered it is not recorded, no apprentice is named, and no named person is met or speaks.

keepsake.text: A fictional note of one apprentice's round with the Democrat of 1 July 1835: where the first copies went and where the last. No real apprentice, wage or delivery is recorded on it.

East along South Water Street, then a block south to Lake and Dearborn.

opening.text:
JAUNT: APPRENTICE AT THE DEMOCRAT. Wednesday, 1 July 1835, and you are thirteen. In May the Chicago Democrat printed: 'Wanted immediately, an apprentice at this office to the printing business'. It added that 'A good opportunity is offered by an immediate application'. You applied immediately. Now you sweep, ink the type, fold the sheets and run, and on Wednesdays you carry the paper through a town that is half boom and half rumour.

The rumour this summer is cholera. It has been in the state, the papers are counting the dead, and everyone who opens your paper looks for that column first. Today's number is under your arm. Where it goes first, and where you linger, is up to you. The places and the papers are real; the apprentice is you.

premise: Play the Chicago Democrat's new apprentice on publication day, 1 July 1835, in a town reading about cholera: choose where the paper goes first and where you linger, and come back to the office with your own story of the morning.

choices.consequence: The river end of town reads the paper first.
choices.label: West to the Sauganash

choices.consequence: You will look at the other paper before anyone sees yours.
choices.label: East to the rival paper

stops.narrative: West to the river, or east to the rival?
stops.text: This corner of South Water and Clark is where John Calhoun printed the first number of the Democrat, on 26 November 1833. The office has moved since: by May it was upstairs over Jones & King's hardware store, along South Water Street, and that is where you work. The paper comes out every Wednesday; today's is No. 11 of its second volume. And since 8 June the town has a second weekly, the Chicago American, out on Saturday mornings, chasing the same readers and the same advertisers.

stops.narrative: Where the town's travellers read the news.
stops.text: West along the river to Lake and Market and the Sauganash. Juliette Kinzie remembered 'a pretentious white two-story building, with bright-blue wooden shutters'. Your own paper looked it over this June and found it repaired, fitted up and furnished with neatness and taste, which is the kind of notice a landlord likes to read. Moses and Kirkland call it 'the most attractive hostlery the city possessed', and Mark Beaubien 'the fiddler par excellence of the town'. When the mail came, 'often irregular and long delayed', somebody would 'mount a dry goods box' and read the news out. Now it is printed, and sold.

stops.narrative: Where the other paper is made.
stops.text: East along South Water Street, near the drawbridge, is the office of the Chicago American, T. O. Davis's paper, three weeks old. Its number of 27 June carries a druggist's notice for the Fire King's Specific, a cholera elixir offered as a certain preventive and cure of the asphyxiated cholera, dated the very day the Democrat printed its own cholera column. That column counted about twenty deaths in three weeks at Alton, chased a rumour it could not trace, and called Chicago uncommonly healthy. One paper sells reassurance, the other sells the cure.

choices.consequence: You will see what comes up the river, and carry it back in your head.
choices.label: Wait for a sail

choices.consequence: The hotel's readers get their paper before noon.
choices.label: On to the Tremont

stops.narrative: Linger at the river, or finish the round?
stops.text: On to the river and Newberry & Dole's warehouse. They have advertised in the Democrat since its first issue, and their card is in today's number on page four: storage, forwarding and commission, agents for the Merchants' Line, dry goods, groceries and provisions. Advertisers like these keep a paper alive. When the schooner Illinois came up through the new harbour cut on 12 July 1834, she was cheered at their wharf. Which bank the warehouse stood on is still argued. You have a few copies left and a morning running out.

stops.narrative: Where the river is crossed, and passed.
stops.text: East to the foot of Dearborn Street and the first drawbridge, which the ship-carpenter Nelson R. Norton began in March 1834. Moses and Kirkland make it '300 feet in length, by sixteen in width', with 'a double draw'; Andreas gives an opening of about sixty feet and gallows frames at either end. Vessels kept striking it, and the town kept paying to patch it, in 1834 and again this year. Every sail that comes up to the wharves passes through this gap, and whatever it carries, cargo or contagion, is news. Stay on the south bank.

Up to Lake and Dearborn and the Tremont House, Alanson Sweet's frame hotel of 1833, kept since 1834 by Ira Couch. Its brick successor of 1850 would be thought so 'absurdly large' that people called it Couch's Folly. Last week's Democrat announced a new auction and commission house on South Water Street, its first public sale set for 'the 1st day of July'. Today, and a first sale is news worth running for.

title: Apprentice at the Democrat
